windows.updaterSub: A real open-source project — but read what it is before you download it.
windows.updaterBody: A developer going by {winAuthor} publishes mirasim-win-updater, an MIT-licensed tool that keeps an existing Windows copy of Mirasim up to date. It works because Mirasim is an Electron shell plus a platform-neutral JavaScript payload: the tool pulls the official payload or extracts the new shell out of the official DMG, then rewrites only the files that changed. It verifies the SHA-256 of everything it downloads and checks the payload's ed25519 signature against the public key taken from the shell.

facts.p: The whole tool is one readable JavaScript file, and you can build the exe yourself in two commands instead of trusting a binary.
SHA-256 on the DMG and the payload, plus ed25519 signature verification on the payload — the same check the app itself does.
Changed and deleted files are backed up first, and --rollback restores the previous version completely.

facts.h: It is an updater, not an installer
facts.p: Its own docs are explicit: it cannot produce a Windows install from scratch, because the Electron runtime and Windows native modules have to come from an install you already have. If you have never had Mirasim on Windows, this tool gives you nothing to run.
Injecting the SEA payload invalidates Node's signature, so the build ships unsigned and SmartScreen will warn on first run.
The author states plainly that it is a personal tool with no connection to Mirasim. Nobody at Mirasim reviews, signs or supports it.

windows.riskTitle: Before you download anything called "Mirasim for Windows"
windows.riskIntro: An unofficial build of a developer tool runs with your permissions, your files and your API keys in reach. Treat every such file as untrusted until you have checked it yourself.
riskPoints: The only files Mirasim itself publishes come from cdn-assets.mirasim.ai. Anything else — however convincing the page looks — is somebody else's build.
Prefer reading the source and building it yourself over running a prebuilt, unsigned exe. This project documents how, and it needs no preinstalled toolchain.
If you do run a third-party binary, do it on a machine that holds no credentials you care about, and never paste API keys into it.
You carry the risk. This wiki links the project because it is open and honest about its limits — that is not a security review, and not an endorsement.
windows.updaterLinks: Source and releases: {winRepo} · latest release. Read the README and the porting notes first — they are candid about what the tool cannot do.

faq.q: Is there an official Mirasim Windows version?
faq.a: No. As of v{version} the official release contains macOS arm64 builds, an Android APK and a VS Code extension. No exe, no msi, no Windows archive.

faq.q: Is the community Windows updater safe?
faq.a: It is open source under MIT, it verifies SHA-256 and an ed25519 signature on what it downloads, and it can roll back — which is more care than most unofficial tools take. It is also unsigned, unaffiliated with Mirasim and unreviewed by them. Read the source or build it yourself, and run it on a machine where a mistake would not cost you credentials.

faq.q: Can that updater install Mirasim on Windows for me?
faq.a: No, and its own documentation says so: it can only update a Windows install that already exists, because the Electron runtime and Windows native modules must be taken from that install. From zero it produces nothing runnable.
Nothing has been announced. The app is in Alpha and macOS-first. This page and the download table update automatically, so if that changes you will see it here.

intro.title: What Mirasim is
intro.sub: One Agent IDE — the agent that writes your code and the simulated user that tests it, in the same workbench.
intro.body: In the usual workflow you write code in one tool, then open the page yourself to check it. Mirasim connects those two ends: coding agents work in parallel inside the workbench, and when a build is ready, simulated users actually use your product in a real browser or a real mobile emulator and bring the first-hand feedback back. These are the core capabilities listed on the official site:

cards.p: Several projects side by side, each with its own sessions, agents and model configuration — nothing bleeds across.
Run many agent sessions at once, with a VS Code-like editor for quick edits. Works from mobile too.

cards.h: Terminal and GUI, one keystroke apart
cards.p: The same workflow either way: keyboard-driven in the TUI, point-and-browse in the GUI.

cards.h: Automation that reads structure, not screenshots
cards.p: The agent reads pages as text structure — roughly 184 B against 60 KB for a screenshot, about 330× less data — driving real Chrome with a real user profile.
Mac apps, the iOS Simulator and the Android emulator answer the same way, so mobile products get tested by simulated users too.

cards.h: A single tool entry saves context
cards.p: The official figure is about 1k tokens of tool overhead per turn, against roughly 53k for thirty tool schemas — the context stays with the work.

intro.callout: Mirasim is in Alpha; the official wording is "expect rough edges". Once installed, the app keeps itself up to date.
